content: The document provides detailed guidelines for assessing and managing children at primary health-care facilities to prevent overweight and obesity, particularly in the context of the double burden of malnutrition. It emphasizes the importance of addressing both undernutrition and overnutrition in children, as these conditions can coexist within the same population or even the same individual. The guidelines are part of the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) framework and were developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2017. They aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for health-care providers to identify, prevent, and manage malnutrition in all its forms. The document includes anthropometric measures, such as weight-for-length/height, body mass index (BMI)-for-age, and mid-upper arm circumference, to classify the nutritional status of children. The classification system defines various categories of malnutrition, including obesity, overweight, moderate and severe underweight, moderate and severe acute malnutrition, and stunting. For example, obesity is defined as a weight-for-length/height or BMI-for-age greater than three standard deviations (SD) above the median of the WHO child growth standards. Severe acute malnutrition is characterized by a weight-for-length/height or BMI-for-age more than three SD below the median, mid-upper arm circumference less than 115 mm, or the presence of bilateral pitting edema. The guidelines also address the care of children with acute or chronic malnutrition, as well as those who are overweight or obese. They provide best practice statements and recommendations for interventions, including nutritional assessment, growth monitoring, and the use of specially formulated foods, such as ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF) and lipid-based nutrient supplements (LNS). These foods are designed to meet the specific nutritional needs of malnourished children and are easy to consume without additional preparation. The document highlights the importance of addressing food insecurity, which is a major cause of poor nutritional status. Food insecurity occurs when individuals lack secure access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food for normal growth and development. It can be chronic, seasonal, or transitory and is often linked to inadequate purchasing power, poor food distribution, and inappropriate feeding practices. The guidelines also discuss the role of metabolic and physiological indicators in assessing the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes mellitus in children. These indicators include abnormal glucose tolerance, elevated hemoglobin A1c, age-related lipid profiles, increased blood pressure, and carotid artery thickness and rigidity. The WHO emphasizes that the guidelines are intended for non-commercial use and should be appropriately cited when adapted or redistributed. The organization does not endorse specific products or services and disclaims liability for any damages arising from the use of the material. The guidelines are subject to periodic updates to incorporate new evidence and ensure their continued relevance and effectiveness. In summary, the document provides a comprehensive framework for the prevention and management of malnutrition in children, with a focus on integrating equity and human rights perspectives into health-care practices. It underscores the need for a holistic approach to addressing the double burden of malnutrition, which includes both undernutrition and overnutrition, to improve the health and well-being of children worldwide.
